extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, propagandists, advertisers, and opinion-shapers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and executing organized propaganda/public-relations campaigns (including press releases, events, media placement and leadership coordination) to shape public opinion and behavior. Emphasizes media selection, group-targeting, credibility, event-creation, and ethical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious and intelligent manipulation of public habits and opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat shaping opinion as an intentional technical activity — plan, research, and execute with knowledge of social mechanisms rather than leaving outcomes to chance. Recognize that leadership and organized effort are necessary to simplify public choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and endurance (continuous effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Modern propaganda is a consistent, enduring effort to create or shape events to influence the relations of the public to an enterprise, idea or group.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda must be sustained over time — one-off actions are rarely sufficient. Campaigns should be persistent and coordinated to produce durable changes in public perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segmenting society and targeting interlocking group structures
rubrics_metrics.description: The propagandist must take account of “the anatomy of society, with its interlocking group formations and loyalties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map social cleavages (political, economic, racial, religious, professional, etc.) and identify channels and leaders within each group. Design messages and tactics tailored to specific group loyalties and cross-group influencers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and enlist opinion leaders/key men
rubrics_metrics.description: Use “key men in every group—persons whose mere word carried authority to hundreds or thousands” to secure cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate and secure the cooperation of respected spokespeople (editors, clergy, association presidents, celebrities, local bosses) whose endorsement multiplies reach and legitimacy; often the minority must work through these leaders to influence the many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create events and circumstances (manufacture news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagandists should “create circumstances and create pictures in the minds of millions” and may “create some of the day’s events” to compete for news attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design staged or facilitated events (reports, exhibitions, endorsements, demonstrations) that have intrinsic news value so editors will cover them; ensure events are credible and tailored to intended media audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the proper media and adapt to shifting media values
rubrics_metrics.description: “The relative value of the various instruments of propaganda, and their relation to the masses, are constantly changing. If he is to get full reach for his message he must take advantage of these shifts of value the instant they occur.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously evaluate and choose among newspapers, magazines, radio, motion pictures, lectures, exhibitions, and emerging media. Match medium to target audience and message form; be ready to reallocate resources as media habits change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create news value and respect editorial selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The propagandist must make ideas take their place among other ideas and events in an editor’s assessment of news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame releases and events to meet editors’ criterion of newsworthiness (timeliness, importance, human interest, authority). Avoid expecting unconditional placement — tailor pitches to specific outlets and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: State sources clearly and present facts accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: “The source of the news offered to the editor should always be clearly stated and the facts accurately presented.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain credibility by transparent sourcing and factual accuracy. Misleading or unverifiable claims risk being discarded by editors and damaging long-term reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish tactics by medium (newspaper vs. magazine vs. radio vs. film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines “select their material deliberately, in accordance with a continuous policy,” while newspapers reflect current news; radio reaches simultaneous mass audiences; motion pictures act as “unconscious carrier[s] of propaganda.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use newspapers for timely news/events, magazines for themed or expert content tied to editorial policy, radio for mass simultaneous reach and sound-based appeals, and films for broad cultural standardization; design content to suit each medium’s format and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personality and manage public figures carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Personality is a central instrument: “The public instinctively demands a personality to typify a conspicuous corporation or enterprise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a consistent outward picture for spokespeople and personalities; exploit personalities to humanize and dramatize messages but avoid scandals or incoherence that undermine credibility. Treat personality as an objective fact to be managed strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek repercussion rather than only direct attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The real value of the lecture, from the propaganda point of view, is in its repercussion to the general public.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities so they generate secondary publicity (reports, broadcasts, social diffusion). Success metrics should include subsequent coverage, social echoes, and behavioral change, not just event turnout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate across geographies and supply chains when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: reviving velvet fashion required contacting Lyons manufactories and Paris couturiers and enlisting a Parisian to influence designers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When influencing tastes or supply-driven markets, act on upstream nodes (manufacturers, designers, influencers in trend centers) and coordinate international or cross-industry partners to create the chain of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research, expert witnesses, and institutional authority for credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports and statements from authoritative sources (State Department, Carnegie Foundation, Hoover report) lend weight and are accepted by the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission or leverage credible research, foundations, experts, or institutional statements to back claims. Attribution to respected institutions increases acceptance among skeptical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret and translate specialized knowledge for the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must “interpret the models of beauty which it possesses” and make their message intelligible to the community they serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume technical or scholarly audiences; translate complex ideas into accessible language, metaphors and narratives that fit public mental pictures and daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect ethical boundaries: avoid deliberate lies and harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda “becomes vicious and reprehensible only when its authors consciously and deliberately disseminate what they know to be lies, or when they aim at effects which they know to be prejudicial to the common good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess campaigns for honesty and public welfare; avoid knowingly false statements and manipulations intended to cause harm. Ethical practice preserves long-term influence and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit emotional habits and mental clichés cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagandists “made use of the mental clichés and the emotional habits of the public to produce mass reactions” during wartime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common emotional frames and stereotypes to make messages resonant, but be aware that exploitation can inflame prejudices and have unintended social consequences; balance emotional appeal with factual grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messaging to accomplish specific practical objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: A widespread desire (e.g., housewives opposing certain foods) must be organized and concentrated upon the state legislature or Congress to be translated into effective legal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define concrete objectives (policy change, purchase behavior, attendance) and design tactics (grassroots organization, lobbying, media pressure) that concentrate public opinion onto decision-makers or purchasing channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of institutional projection rather than passive reception
rubrics_metrics.description: An institution (museum) should not be evaluated merely by visitors but must “project itself and what it stands for in the community which it serves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should take active leadership roles (councils, research boards, outreach) to shape standards and public taste rather than solely receiving public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tactics to audience habits and competing attractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public meetings once led in value; now automobiles, radio, and newspaper editions have changed attendance habits and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize audience time, attention, and competing media. If a traditional tactic no longer draws, replace it with alternatives that fit contemporary lifestyles and consumption patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expecting editorial immunity; accept editors’ independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors “determine with complete independence what is and what is not news” and may discard items irrespective of interest to the propagandist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build relationships and craft genuinely newsworthy material; avoid presuming placement. Use multiple channels and create events that naturally fit news criteria to increase chances of editorial pick-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure success by public acceptance and behavioral change
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda’s function is to “create public acceptance for a particular idea or commodity” and to regiment the public mind as effectively as an army might regiment bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns on whether they change public mental pictures, increase acceptance, alter behavior, or influence policy — not just short-term metrics like impressions or attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combined appeals (visual, graphic, auditory) and coordinated channels
rubrics_metrics.description: During the war, campaigns appealed “to the individual by means of every approach—visual, graphic, and auditory” and secured cooperation of key men in groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synchronize messages across formats (imagery, copy, speeches, broadcasts) and channel types to reinforce the same idea; coordinate timing so multiple channels amplify each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to new technology and formats (television, broadcasting, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The propagandist “must be alert to make use of all the means of propaganda,” including new avenues like television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously scan for emerging technologies and evaluate their potential for reach and persuasion; pilot and integrate promising platforms into strategy early.
